name: Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge
title: Pattern 7: Speech as a Bridge
answer: Speech as a Bridge is the seventh of the book's ten patterns, and it uses speech technology to give students a way around a barrier rather than a way past the learning itself. Text to speech reads a page aloud to a student who struggles with print, speech to text lets a student with a writing disability say what they know, and live captions serve students who are deaf or hard of hearing as well as English learners following a fast lecture. It matters because the same tool can either carry a student through a subject or quietly replace a skill they still need to be taught, and that choice belongs to people, not software.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: The pattern treats speech technology as a bridge that opens doors for students whose reading, writing or hearing gets in the way of the lesson. A student who cannot decode a page can still hear it, and a student who cannot produce written text can still speak an answer, so the content of the lesson stays within reach. Live captions do similar work in a lecture that moves too quickly to follow by ear alone, whether the reason is hearing loss or a second language. Several of these supports can sit in one place, as they do in tools such as Microsoft Immersive Reader. The problem it solves is access: without a bridge, the barrier rather than the subject decides what a student learns.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In preschool and the early grades, speech tools appear as read aloud practice and fluency feedback, where a child reads and the tool responds. With older students the bridge widens: text to speech carries a student through a subject such as history when print is the obstacle, and speech to text lets a student with a writing disability put what they know into words. Live captions serve students who are deaf or hard of hearing and English learners who are trying to keep up with a fast lecture. Tools such as Microsoft Immersive Reader gather several of these supports into a single place so a student does not have to assemble them alone. Across all of these uses the same question returns: is the tool providing access to the lesson, or standing in for a skill the student still needs to be taught?
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence for the early grades as a call for patience. A six week study of an AI voice tutor with children aged 3 to 7 found that it delivered the literacy activities as consistently as parents did, but children learned more when a parent read with them (Quan et al., 2026). The same study found the tool struggled to understand young children's speech, so a parent or teacher still had to listen closely. On the question of when to use the bridge, researchers describe strategic offloading, which means using the tool for access while still teaching the skill the tool replaces (Seung & Basham, 2026).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book sets the central limit as a question rather than a rule: when to use the bridge and when to build the skill. A student with a reading disability may need text to speech to learn history, but may also need direct reading instruction without it, and both needs can sit side by side. The individualized education program team, not the software, decides which is which for each student. In the early grades the tool's difficulty understanding young children's speech means an adult still has to listen closely rather than hand the work over. The decisions about access and instruction therefore stay with people who know the student.
